_comment: Devpost Codegeist 2026 'Additional info' step. The values for every submission requirement field, keyed by the field index shown in the form URL. Kept in the repo so the form can be filled from a single source and reproduced if it has to be resubmitted.
8:
Install the app with the installation link above. A Jira site administrator has to do this; the app is unlicensed and free, so there is no billing involved and no credentials are needed.

1. Open any Jira issue and click View app actions → AgentLedger. The panel appears on the right of the issue view.
2. Paste the agent reference JyP9X278CKWoNLAFg5kVr and press Verify. The app calls the Concordium Agent Registry (CIS-8004) live over HTTPS and shows every individual check it performed: on-chain agent found, status active, agent URI present, card fetched, card hash matches the hash committed on chain, badge present, owner matches, contracts match, extension conformant. A second identity source, an ERC-8004 registry on Base Sepolia, is read directly over eth_call.
3. Press Record with an action such as 'Comment on an issue'. The attestation is appended to the trail. Then try 'Trigger a refund / payout': it is recorded as flagged (human-gated) and the agent is not allowed to proceed. The panel shows the trail and its chain state.
4. Open the AgentLedger Auditor agent in Jira (Rovo) and ask it to show the attestation trail for the issue. It answers from the trail, not from its own memory of the conversation: it confirms chainValid, names the agent and its registry id, and states that a human must approve before the refund proceeds.
5. If you have an MCP client, connect it to the app's MCP server and call the five tools: AgentLedger action policy, Verify agent identity, Work item context, Read the attestation trail, Record an agent action.

Notes for judges: the Teamwork Graph scopes (read:graph:*) are optional, without them the graph queries return empty, the app says so plainly, and everything else keeps working. The demo video (https://youtu.be/tKIMEUkLjo4) shows the whole flow on a real issue, and the source is at https://github.com/llakterian/agentledger-forge.
10:
Build an app using Atlassian's Forge platform and integrate with at least one Atlassian product or platform capability.

AgentLedger is a Forge app on nodejs24.x integrating with three Atlassian capabilities:

1. Jira (jira:issuePanel). The panel lives on the issue view and reads the issue key from view.getContext(), verified live on issue KAN-1 and KAN-5.
2. Teamwork Graph (read:graph:* scopes), via api.asUser().requestTeamworkGraph() through the manifest's egress rules, so the acting user's own permissions apply. Where the site's graph schema does not expose a field (the Teamwork Graph API is in Early Access), the app reports exactly that instead of failing.
3. Rovo (rovo:agent, rovo:mcp, rovo:skill). An agent with five tools, a reusable skill, and an MCP server reachable from third-party MCP clients.

The app is not a wrapper around a language model: the model is optional, the policy table and the hash chain are plain code, and every decision the app makes is enforced in the backend rather than in the UI or in prompt text.
12:
AgentLedger is built for the industries where an automated action on a case has to be defensible later: financial services, healthcare, insurance, logistics and public administration. In those settings the questions are not 'how good is the model' but 'which agent was this, what was it allowed to do, and who approved it'.

The app answers exactly those questions. Identity comes from a registry the agent does not control (a Concordium CIS-8004 agent registry on-chain, plus an ERC-8004 registry read over eth_call), with the card hash compared against the hash committed on chain and every individual check shown. Authority comes from a policy table in code, so a refund, an approval or a closure is human-gated rather than merely discouraged in a prompt. Evidence comes from a hash-chained attestation trail, so an entry cannot be edited or removed without the break being visible and located.

That combination, verifiable identity, least-authority action, human approval for the irreversible actions, and an audit trail, is the compliance shape that specialized industries require, and it is what the app demonstrates end to end.
15:
What worked well was the loop, not the abstractions. `forge deploy --non-interactive` into a real environment and then exercising the app inside Jira gave a much faster signal than reading documentation, and the parts that carry the risk. The policy engine, the hash chain, the route builders, the encoding helpers, are pure code with no Atlassian dependency, so they are covered by 40 unit tests that run without an account. A local manifest validator cross-checks every declared action input against the keys the backend actually reads, which is how a mismatch between the manifest and the code gets caught before a judge ever sees it.

What was hard was the shape of the runtime calls. Forge passes a module resolver { context, call: { functionKey, payload } }, not (payload, context), so reading payload.op off the first argument returns undefined and every panel operation silently falls through to a default branch that answers something plausible. @forge/kvs is CommonJS, so a default import can land on the whole module.exports namespace and surface at runtime as 'kvs.get is not a function'. And @forge/api v6 removed asUser().get(); a Jira read is now api.asUser().requestJira(route), where the route must be built with the `route` tagged template, passing a plain string fails at runtime with "You must create your route using the 'route' export from '@forge/api'".

The common thread is that none of these raise an error where you would look for one: each produces a well-formed wrong answer. The fix in every case was the same, make the call shape explicit, assert it locally, and fail loudly at the point of use. Two of those checks are now permanent guards in the validator, so they cannot come back.

Also worth knowing for anyone building on Forge: a jira:issuePanel module receives every invoke at the module resolver regardless of the function key, so the panel has to route its own operations explicitly; and an MCP tool is called with exactly the inputs the manifest declares, so reading an undeclared key returns undefined with no error anywhere.
16: OpenCode. An open-source AI coding agent, running the MiniMax M3.1 Flash model, was the main build tool. It wrote the resolver and its dispatcher, the KVS client resolution, the route builders and the test suite, and it drove the browser (the Atlassian developer console, Jira, Rovo and Devpost) to find and verify the runtime bugs described above rather than trusting the code to a green test run alone. The Rovo agent inside the product ('AgentLedger Auditor') is part of the application itself, not a build tool. No other AI tooling was used to write the code.
